You are a research scout for the Fortress-revival project (Sun/Oracle's Fortress language, Guy Steele, 2003–2012). Audience: the main session, which is drafting a repository README whose "Papers" section labels several in-repo LaTeX papers as "unpublished draft" / "submission draft" / "notes". Your job: search the public record (DBLP, ACM DL, Google Scholar, arXiv, author pages, Semantic Scholar) with WebSearch/WebFetch and determine for EACH item below whether it — or a close descendant with substantially the same content/title — was ever actually published (venue, year, final title, authors), or whether "unpublished draft" is accurate.

Items (titles as they appear in the repo's Papers/ tree, all Sun Labs Programming Language Research group, ca. 2010–2012):

1. "Implementing Fully Modular, Statically Typed, Symmetric Multimethod Dispatch" — Guy Steele, David Chase, et al.; internally a POPL 2011 submission. Did any version appear at POPL or elsewhere?
2. "Welterweight Fortress" / "Dynamic Dispatch and Type Inference Semipredicates" — David Chase, Justin Hilburn, Victor Luchangco, et al. Any publication of a "Welterweight Fortress" calculus?
3. "Enforcing Fortress' Return Type Rule at Runtime" (run-time instantiation of generics / return type rule). Check especially later descendants by Sukyoung Ryu's group with Steele, e.g. "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance" (POPL 2019?) — is that a descendant of this line, and does any paper with substantially THIS content exist in print?
4. A journal-version draft of the OOPSLA 2011 paper "Type Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance" (Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, Steele) focused on the return type rule — did a journal version ever appear (TOPLAS, JFP, Science of Computer Programming...)?
5. Implementation notes: "Fortress function and method encodings" and "Mapping Fortress type relationships onto the JVM type system" — any workshop/venue publication (e.g. VMIL, JVM languages workshop)?

Also confirm the OOPSLA 2011 paper itself (item 4's conference version) is correctly attributed — venue and author list.

Method: verify against primary sources (DBLP entries, ACM DL pages); do not trust a single search snippet. Distinguish "same paper published" vs "related but distinct later work". Cross-check DBLP pages for Guy L. Steele Jr., David Chase, Victor Luchangco, Sukyoung Ryu, Karl Naden, Justin Hilburn, Scott Kilpatrick around 2010–2020.

Return raw findings as your final text: for each of the 5 items, a verdict (PUBLISHED at <venue year> / UNPUBLISHED as far as the record shows / RELATED WORK EXISTS: <cite>, distinct content), with the URLs/DBLP keys you verified against, and any uncertainty flagged. Terse, factual, no preamble.

## Key Findings

**Fortress and Symmetric Multiple Dispatch:**
Fortress faced significant difficulties in implementing its sophisticated type system on virtual machines such as the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), where mismatches between the language's design ambitions—such as symmetric multimethod dispatch—and the underlying runtime environment proved insurmountable without substantial further investment.

**Modularity Challenges:**
A major obstacle to adding symmetric multimethods to an existing statically-typed programming language has been their modularity problem: independently-developed modules, which typecheck in isolation, may cause type errors when combined.

**Previous Approaches:**
Previous work on adding multimethods to an existing statically-typed object-oriented language has either been done by forcing global typechecking or by employing asymmetric multiple dispatch in order to ensure safety of modular typechecking.

## Key Research

Previous work on statically typed multimethods whose arguments are treated symmetrically required the whole program to be available for typechecking. However, Dubious is a core language including first-class generic functions with symmetric multimethods and modules that can be separately typechecked.

Two sets of restrictions ensure modular type safety for Dubious, as well as an interesting intermediate point between these two.

## The Challenge

A major obstacle to adding symmetric multimethods to an existing statically-typed programming language has been their modularity problem: independently-developed modules, which typecheck in isolation, may cause type errors when combined.

## Practical Implementation: MultiJava

MultiJava is a backward-compatible extension to Java supporting open classes and symmetric multiple dispatch, with previous theoretical work adapted to allow compilation units to be statically typechecked modularly and safely, ruling out any link-time or run-time type errors.

Multimethods offer several advantages including a simple solution to the binary method problem, a natural implementation of the strategy design pattern, and a form of open objects that enables easy addition of new operations to existing classes.
